title: When, then
hook: "when X happens, I will do Y" plans had medium-to-large effects in a review of the research (Gollwitzer and Sheeran)

segments.voice: Yesterday, less friction: make the good thing one step easier. Was the path already open when you woke up? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-eight.

"I'll meditate more." It's said on New Year's Eve, on Sunday nights, after a good retreat. It's sincere. And by Wednesday it has quietly evaporated. Now try a different sentence: "When I set my coffee cup down after breakfast, then I'll sit for two minutes." Same hope. Different shape. The first sentence is a wish floating in the air. The second has an address and a time of arrival. Psychologists have a name for that second kind of sentence, and they have measured what the shape does. Today's word is the small hinge it turns on.
screen: `I'LL MEDITATE MORE.` → `GONE BY WEDNESDAY.` → `WHEN THIS, THEN THAT.`

segments.voice: First, the shape. Psychologist Peter Gollwitzer called these plans implementation intentions: when this situation arrives, then I will do that. A goal says what. An implementation intention says when, where and how. Second, why it works. The plan hands the decision to the moment ahead of time. When the situation shows up, there's nothing left to decide. The cue from earlier this week is doing the work again: the when becomes the cue, and the then becomes the routine. Third, the measurement. Gollwitzer and Paschal Sheeran gathered the studies of these plans into one review, and found the effect on whether people followed through was medium to large, by the usual yardstick researchers use. For something as small as one sentence, that is a real effect. Fourth, an old shape. Some traditions tied practice to set moments of the day long before the research. In the Psalms, the King James Bible has the line: "Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice." Evening, morning, noon. Not "more often." Three appointments with a when. And this week has been building toward exactly this. Ten minutes on the breath. Attention, trainable. Almost half of a day running on habit. The cue at the start of the loop. The place that holds it. Less friction. Today's hinge ties them together: a when, a where, a small then. That's how a hope becomes something that actually happens on an ordinary day.
screen: `WHEN THIS, THEN THAT.` · `THE DECISION, MADE AHEAD.` · `MEDIUM TO LARGE.` · then, large: `EVENING, AND MORNING, AND AT NOON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one when-then plan, in your head for now. Sit and settle on the breath. Then think of a moment that already happens every day: setting down your keys, the kettle clicking off, the car engine going quiet. That's your when. Now choose a small then: three breaths, one minute of sitting, one line you value read slowly. Say the whole sentence silently, once: "When this, then that." Picture the moment arriving, and you doing it. Then let it go and rest on the breath. The bell holds the time.
When. The first half of a when-then plan, which ties a small practice to a moment that already happens. Today's word.

Your line: when, then. Today, write your sentence down somewhere you'll see it, on paper or in your phone. When the moment comes, let the plan do the deciding. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: People who want a practice to stick sometimes write it as a when-then plan, tying it to a moment that already happens each day; some religious traditions also set prayer or practice at fixed times of day.

what a scholar hears: Gollwitzer's implementation intentions turn a situation into a cue, and the pooled research found medium-to-large effects on follow-through.
